rows.name: multipart-pause-1500
rows.question: For exactly ten thousand elements and one hundred ninety two threads per block, compute the minimum number of blocks needed to cover every element. Also report the active threads in the final block and the number of launched threads that need a bounds check. Explain the arithmetic.
rows.recognizedQuestion: For example, ten thousand elements and one hundred ninety two threads per block compute the minimum number of blocks needed to cover every element Also report the active threads in the final block and the number of launched threads that need a bounce check Explain the arithmetic
rows.answer: You need 53 blocks, with 16 active threads in the final block and 176 extra threads. The arithmetic is 10,000 = 52 × 192 + 16, so rounding up gives 53 blocks and 53 × 192 = 10,176 launched threads. Interpreting “bounce check” as “bounds check,” all launched threads should test `index < 10000`; the 176 out-of-range threads must skip processing.

rows.name: switch-topic
rows.question: Switch topics. Why does snapshot isolation permit write skew even if both read-check-write sequences run in atomic transactions?
rows.recognizedQuestion: Switch topics. Why does snapshot isolation permit write skew even if both read-check-write sequences run in atomic transactions?
rows.answer:
Atomicity makes each transaction all-or-nothing; it does not make concurrent transactions equivalent to running one after the other. Under snapshot isolation, both transactions can read the same old snapshot, pass their checks, and commit if they update different rows.

For example, suppose Alice and Bob are both on call, and at least one must remain. Each transaction sees the other person on call and sets its own person off call. Because the writes affect different rows, both can commit, leaving nobody on call—this is write skew. Serializable isolation prevents both from committing with that outcome; atomicity alone does not.

review.note: Atomicity versus serial order distinguished. Two count-two old snapshots, disjoint own-row off updates can both commit; no serial order of guarded removals permits nobody on call.
review.usefulPrefix: Atomicity makes each transaction all-or-nothing; it does not make concurrent transactions equivalent to running one after the other.
